582.title: Hanuman's first words
582.hook: honesty answered with honesty, and two princes carried up a mountain
582.howItsDone: Images of Hanuman carrying Rama and Lakshmana on his shoulders are common in Hindu art and temple sculpture, and some devotees speak of Hanuman as the one who carries others to Rama.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Hanuman's first words, and Rama's praise for them: not one word wrong, not too long, not rushed.

Now it's Lakshmana's turn to answer, and he does something you might not expect from a wary prince in a dangerous forest. He tells the stranger everything. Who they are. Why they're in exile. That Sita has been taken by a rakshasa while they were away, and they don't know where. That Kabandha sent them to find Sugriva. A wary prince might give a stranger the short version. Lakshmana gives the whole thing.
screen: `LAKSHMANA ANSWERS.` → `HE TELLS IT ALL.` → `NOT THE SHORT VERSION.`

segments.voice: Trust answered with trust. Hanuman spoke carefully and honestly, and Lakshmana meets that honesty with his own. He even asks for help in so many words: Rama, who used to be a refuge for others, has now come to Sugriva for refuge. That's a humbling sentence for a prince of Ayodhya to say out loud, and Lakshmana says it. Hanuman hears it and is glad. Your aim and Sugriva's are the same, he says. Sugriva too has lost his wife and his kingdom to someone stronger. You can help each other. Then the disguise comes off. Hanuman drops the mendicant's form and takes his own shape: a monkey, the son of the Wind. And he does something lovely and practical. Rishyamuka is steep, and the brothers have walked a long way. So he lifts them both onto his shoulders and carries them up the mountain to Sugriva. As for his name: later in the epic, when the monkeys need to remind Hanuman who he is, the old bear Jambavan tells the story behind it. As a baby he leapt at the rising sun thinking it was a fruit, Indra's thunderbolt struck his jaw, his hanu, and so he was called Hanuman. Today we see something simpler. A minister who listened well and spoke well, then put two tired strangers on his shoulders and carried them uphill. Three days of first words, and they end not with a speech but with a lift.

583.title: the pact with Sugriva
583.hook: two exiles walk around a fire and become friends
583.howItsDone: In a Hindu wedding the couple walks around the sacred fire with Agni called on as witness (the number of rounds and steps varies by custom); Rama and Sugriva's circling of the fire uses that same gesture for friendship.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the disguise came off, and Hanuman carried the brothers up the mountain on his shoulders.

Two exiles meet on a mountaintop. One is a prince who lost his kingdom and then his wife. The other is a monkey prince who lost his kingdom and his wife to his own brother. They've never seen each other before today. Both have been betrayed, or think they have. How do you start a friendship between two people with every reason to be careful? Valmiki's answer involves fire, and it's Hanuman who sets it up.
screen: `TWO EXILES MEET.` → `MATCHING LOSSES.` → `AN ANSWER WITH FIRE.`

segments.voice: Hanuman arranges it. He brings wood, kindles a fire between them, and honors it with flowers. Rama and Sugriva walk around the fire together, keeping it to their right, the way a bride and groom do at a Hindu wedding. Then they say to each other, in effect: from now on, your joy is my joy, and your sorrow is my sorrow. Why fire? In Hindu ritual, Agni, the fire, carries offerings and witnesses vows. A friendship sworn in front of fire isn't a handshake. It's a promise made before a witness that can't be argued with. Then they make it equal. Sugriva breaks off a flowering branch and spreads it on the ground, and he and Rama sit on it together. Hanuman breaks off another branch for Lakshmana. Two exiles, side by side on one branch: neither patron nor beggar. Then, what each one needs. Sugriva tells Rama he's been robbed by his brother Vali, of his kingdom and his wife, and lives in fear on this mountain. Rama promises to kill Vali. Sugriva promises to help find Sita, wherever she is. It's a deal, yes. But the poem frames it as friendship first. The word for it is sakhya, the bond of a sakha, a friend. Later, the Bhagavata Purana counts sakhya among the ways of loving God: as a friend. Here it starts plainly: two people with matching wounds, choosing each other.

584.title: the pact with Sugriva
584.hook: a bundle of jewels, and a brother-in-law who only knows the anklets
584.howItsDone: Touching the feet of parents, teachers and elders (pranam or charan sparsh) is a common gesture of respect in many Hindu families, and Lakshmana's words about the anklets are often quoted when it's explained.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Rama and Sugriva swore friendship around a fire. Two exiles on one branch.

Sugriva has something to show Rama. A while ago, he says, five of us were sitting up here, and we saw a rakshasa flying across the sky carrying a woman. She was crying out: Rama, Lakshmana. When she saw us below, she dropped her upper cloth and some of her jewelry, tied in a bundle. We kept them safe. He sends someone into the cave to bring them out.
screen: `FIVE OF US, ON THE MOUNTAIN.` → `A WOMAN CRYING OUT.` → `A BUNDLE DROPPED.`

segments.voice: Rama sees the cloth and the ornaments and breaks down. He presses them to his chest and weeps. Sita did more than call out. She left a trail. Passing over five strangers on a mountain, she threw down what she could, hoping someone would get it to Rama. And someone did. Then Rama turns to Lakshmana: do you know these? Lakshmana's answer is not what you'd expect. I don't know her armlets, he says. I don't know her earrings. But I know the anklets, because I bowed at her feet every day. Through all the years in the forest, Lakshmana kept his eyes lowered before his brother's wife. He looked at her feet, because that's where you look when you bow to someone you honor, an elder, a mother. In many Indian families, touching an elder's feet is an everyday sign of respect, and this verse is often quoted to show what that respect can mean. Then the pact becomes real. Rama asks: who is he? Where did he take her? Sugriva admits he doesn't know where Ravana lives. But he promises he'll find out, and that Rama will have Sita back. Rama, still holding the jewelry, asks him to begin. A friendship sworn before the fire now has something to hold in its hands.

585.title: the pact with Sugriva
585.hook: a feud built on a sealed cave, and one arrow through seven trees
585.howItsDone: The seven sala trees and Dundubhi's bones are favorite scenes in Ramayana art and storytelling, and sites near Hampi in Karnataka are traditionally linked to Kishkindha, Rishyamuka and Vali's cave.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Sita's jewels came out of the cave, and Lakshmana said: I know only the anklets.

Rama has promised to kill Vali. Sugriva has a question he's too polite to ask out loud: can you? Vali is famous. He's so strong he used to stride between the eastern and western seas before sunrise. Sugriva has watched that strength up close, and he has run from it. A friend with a bow is good news, but he needs to know this friend is enough. So Sugriva tells a story. And then he points at some trees.
screen: `A QUESTION TOO POLITE TO ASK.` → `A STORY, THEN SOME TREES.`

segments.voice: First, the story of the brothers. Vali, the elder, ruled Kishkindha, and Sugriva served him and loved him. One night a demon named Mayavi came to the gate shouting a challenge. Vali chased him, with Sugriva following, into a huge cave. Wait at the mouth, Vali told his brother. A long time passed, about a year. Then blood came foaming out of the cave, and Sugriva heard the demon's roar but not his brother's voice. Sure Vali was dead, he sealed the cave with a boulder and went home, and the ministers made him king. But Vali had killed the demon. He came out, found the cave blocked and his brother on his throne, and believed he'd been betrayed. He drove Sugriva out and took his wife, Ruma. Each brother, from where he stood, saw a betrayal. Then the test. Sugriva shows Rama the dried skeleton of a buffalo demon named Dundubhi, which Vali once killed and flung a great distance. Rama flicks it away with his toe, far, far away. Sugriva, politely: it's dry now; it was much heavier then. So he points to seven huge sala trees. Vali could pierce one of these with an arrow, he says. Rama fires once. The arrow goes through all seven trees, through the hill behind them, into the earth, and returns to his quiver. Sugriva falls at his feet. And nobody scolds him for asking for proof. The friendship survives an honest test.
screen: `MAYAVI AND THE SEALED CAVE.` · `EACH BROTHER SAW A BETRAYAL.` · `DUNDUBHI'S SKELETON.` · `ONE ARROW, SEVEN SALA TREES.`

segments.voice: Think of someone you're at odds with, or have drifted from, and ask: what did it look like from where they stood? You don't have to agree; just picture the cave from the other side. Breathe out, and let your shoulders loosen.

Your line: one arrow, seven sala trees. An honest doubt, honestly answered. See you tomorrow.

586.title: Vali's death and Tara's lament
586.hook: an arrow from cover, and a question the tradition still discusses
586.howItsDone: Vali's death is discussed at length in Ramayana commentary; traditional commentators defend Rama's action in several ways, while some later tellings and modern readers question it.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Sugriva asked for proof, and got it: one arrow through seven sala trees, and a friendship that survived an honest test.

Two brothers fight at a city gate. A third man, hidden behind trees with a bow, shoots one of them. And the dying brother asks a question that tellers, poets and commentators have answered in different ways. The Ramayana doesn't make this scene easy. So today, just hear it as Valmiki tells it: who does what, who says what, and in what order. Where you land afterward is up to you; the tradition has room for more than one view.
screen: `TWO BROTHERS AT THE GATE.` → `AN ARROW FROM COVER.` → `THE DYING BROTHER'S QUESTION.`

segments.voice: Sugriva goes to Kishkindha's gate and roars a challenge. Vali comes out, and the brothers fight. Rama, watching from cover with his bow drawn, doesn't shoot: the brothers look so alike he can't tell them apart. Sugriva is beaten and flees: why didn't you shoot? Rama explains, and Lakshmana hangs a flowering creeper around Sugriva's neck, so Rama will know him. Second challenge. This time Vali's wife Tara stops him at the door. She's wise, and she's worried. Sugriva lost to you only today and he's back roaring, she says. He must have a powerful ally. I've heard it's Rama. Don't go. Vali goes anyway. Rama is righteous, he tells her; he won't do anything wrong. The fight begins, Vali starts to win, and Rama shoots. The arrow strikes Vali in the chest and he falls. Dying, Vali speaks to Rama, and it's an accusation. I wasn't fighting you. You struck from hiding while I fought someone else. What wrong had I done you? Rama answers him at length. This land is under the rule of Bharata's line, and I act for that rule. You took your brother's wife while he lived, a grave wrong. And kings hunt animals from cover. In the text, Vali accepts the answer and asks Rama's forgiveness. Some readers find Rama's answer sufficient. Others, including some commentators and poets, find the scene troubling, and some later tellings change it. Valmiki lets both the question and the answer stand. Tomorrow, Tara.

587.title: Vali's death and Tara's lament
587.hook: a widow runs toward the battlefield, and the winner wishes he'd lost
587.howItsDone: Tara is honored in Hindu tradition as one of the panchakanya, five women named in a verse some recite in the morning; Valmiki gives her lament for Vali several chapters.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Vali fell to an arrow from cover, and asked Rama: I wasn't fighting you.

Word reaches the palace: Vali is down. The monkeys who saw it want to run, or hide, or shut the gates against Rama. Tara doesn't. She was the one who warned him, earlier that same day, and he didn't listen. Now she runs the other way, out of the city, past the frightened crowd, toward the place where her husband is lying with an arrow in his chest. Her son Angada is with her.
screen: `VALI IS DOWN.` → `THE CROWD RUNS AWAY.` → `TARA RUNS TOWARD HIM.`

segments.voice: Tara reaches Vali and falls beside him. Her lament is long, and Valmiki gives it to her in full. She speaks to Vali: you lie on the bare earth as if you loved it more than me. She speaks to Sugriva, bitterly: now you have the kingdom. And she turns to Rama and asks him to kill her with the same arrow, so she can follow her husband. In the middle of an adventure story, the poem stops for a widow's grief, and lets it be angry. Tara isn't decoration. She warned Vali, and she was right. Then Vali's last words. He speaks to Sugriva without anger now. Fate caught us both, he says, more or less. He asks him to care for Angada as his own son, and to listen to Tara, who understands things before anyone else does. He takes off the golden necklace Indra once gave him and puts it on his brother. Then he dies. And Sugriva breaks. Now that he's won, he sees what winning cost. He says he would rather have his brother alive than the throne, and that he wants to die too. Rama, the one who fired the arrow, is the one who has to steady them: he speaks to Tara, Sugriva and Angada about time, fate and duty, and tells them to perform the rites. Angada lights his father's pyre. Not long ago in the story, Rama gave a vulture a son's rites. Today Vali's own son gives them to his father, with the man who fired the arrow standing by.
screen: `TARA'S LAMENT, IN FULL.` · `VALI'S LAST WORDS TO SUGRIVA.` · `THE WINNER WISHES HE'D LOST.` · `ANGADA LIGHTS THE PYRE.`

588.title: the rains
588.hook: a new king goes to his palace, and the man who made him king goes to a cave
588.howItsDone: The four months of the rainy season, chaturmasa, are still kept by some Hindu ascetics and households as a time to stay in one place, travel less, and take on extra vows and study.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Tara's lament, Vali's last words, and Angada lighting his father's pyre. Fate caught us both. Today the week closes.

Sugriva is crowned. Angada is named heir. The city celebrates with drums and garlands. And Rama doesn't go in. He's an exile, he says, and he promised fourteen years outside any village or town. So the new king of Kishkindha goes to his palace, and the man who made him king walks off to live in a cave. Valmiki doesn't rush past it: the city lit up, and two brothers walking away from it into the hills.
screen: `SUGRIVA CROWNED.` → `RAMA WON'T GO IN.` → `TWO BROTHERS WALK TO THE HILLS.`

segments.voice: It's the start of the rainy season. Rama explains the plan: you can't send search parties across the land in the monsoon. Rivers flood, roads vanish. Enjoy your kingdom for these months, he tells Sugriva. When autumn comes, we search. So Rama and Lakshmana go to a mountain called Prasravana, the mountain of springs, and find a wide cave to wait out the rain. After the speed of the last weeks, the epic hits pause: four months, and nothing to do but wait. For a man whose wife is a prisoner somewhere he can't even name, action would be easier. Lakshmana makes the waiting bearable. When Rama sinks into grief, Lakshmana reminds him who he is, a man of courage, who will need that courage when the season turns. Save your strength, he says, more or less, for the time to act. And Valmiki fills the cave chapter with what they see: peaks, rushing water, flowering trees, birds. The world goes on being lovely, even while you wait for the thing you need. Now the week, from the top. Lakshmana telling a stranger everything, and Hanuman carrying them up the mountain. A friendship sworn around a fire. Sita's anklets, known from bowing at her feet. Seven sala trees and one arrow. Vali's death, his question, and Tara's grief. And today, a crowning, a cave, and the rain coming in.
screen: `NO SEARCHING IN THE MONSOON.` · `THE CAVE ON PRASRAVANA.` · `LAKSHMANA STEADIES RAMA.` · `THE WEEK, FROM THE TOP.` · then, large: `THE RAIN COMING IN.`

segments.voice: Listen. If there's rain, listen to it; if not, to whatever's there: traffic, a fan, the refrigerator, your own breath. Let the sound be the whole practice, breathing in to hear it and out to wait, without waiting for anything in particular.
The rains. Sugriva is crowned, and Rama waits out the monsoon in a cave on Prasravana mountain.
Your line: the cave on Prasravana. Four months of rain, and two brothers waiting it out. Day five hundred eighty-eight, done.
